t:
(a) Definition.—In this section—
        (1) the term “Director” means the Director of the Office of Management and Budget; and 
        (2) the term “executive agency” has the meaning given that term in section 105 of title 5, United States Code.  
    (b) OMB Directive.—The Director shall issue a directive to require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to develop a comprehensive software licensing policy, which shall—
        (1) identify clear roles, responsibilities, and central oversight authority within the executive agency for managing enterprise software license agreements and commercial software licenses; and 
        (2) require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to—
            (A) establish a comprehensive inventory, including 80 percent of software license spending and enterprise licenses in the executive agency, by identifying and collecting information about software license agreements using automated discovery and inventory tools; 
            (B) regularly track and maintain software licenses to assist the executive agency in implementing decisions throughout the software license management life cycle; 
            (C) analyze software usage and other data to make cost-effective decisions; 
            (D) provide training relevant to software license management; 
            (E) establish goals and objectives of the software license management program of the executive agency; and 
            (F) consider the software license management life cycle phases, including the requisition, reception, deployment and maintenance, retirement, and disposal phases, to implement effective decisionmaking and incorporate existing standards, processes, and metrics.   
    (c) Report on Software License Management.—
        (1) In general.—Beginning in the first fiscal year beginning after the date of enactment of this Act, and in each of the following 5 fiscal years, the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency shall submit to the Director a report on the financial savings or avoidance of spending that resulted from improved software license management. 
        (2) Availability.—The Director shall make each report submitted under paragraph (1) publically available.

fable.w: Every actor here is inside the federal government: the OMB Director issues a directive to agency Chief Information Officers, who report back to the Director. The tempting reading is that the OMB directive resembles rulemaking or that making the reports publicly available involves the public, but an internal directive is not a regulation with public comment, and publishing reports is one-way disclosure rather than consultation before a decision. No outside party is consulted, sits on a body, or is given a right to object or sue.
fable.s: The Director shall issue a directive to require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to develop a comprehensive software licensing policy

qwen_block.w: This section mandates internal administrative actions within the federal government. The Director of OMB (a federal official) directs Chief Information Officers of executive agencies (federal employees/agencies) to create policies and submit reports. There is no requirement to consult with, coordinate with, or allow participation from any party outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private companies) in the decision-making process. The publication of reports is a transparency measure, not a participatory mechanism.
qwen_block.s: The Director shall issue a directive to require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to develop a comprehensive software licensing policy

opus.w: Every actor here is federal: the OMB Director gives a directive to agency Chief Information Officers, who report back to the Director. The directive is internal management guidance, not rulemaking with public comment. Making the reports publicly available is only disclosure, so no outside party takes part in any federal decision.
opus.s: The Director shall issue a directive to require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to develop a comprehensive software licensing policy
opus.b:
1. **Reasoning.** It's tempting to read "issue a directive" as rulemaking, or to treat making reports "publically available" as public involvement. Neither works. The directive is internal management guidance from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to agency Chief Information Officers. It is not a regulation that would trigger notice and comment. Publishing the reports only shares information with the public; it doesn't let the public take part in any decision. Everyone named in the section — the OMB Director, the Chief Information Officers and the executive agencies — works inside the federal government.

2. **Label.**

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates internal administrative actions within the federal government. The Director of OMB (a federal official) issues directives to Chief Information Officers of executive agencies (federal entities) to develop internal policies and submit reports. There is no requirement to consult, coordinate with, or seek input from any party outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, the public, or private companies) before making these decisions. The public availability of the final report is a transparency measure, not a participatory decision-making process.
qwen_chat.s: The Director shall issue a directive to require the Chief Information Officer of each executive agency to develop a comprehensive software licensing policy
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the reports are made "publically available," this constitutes public participation. However, the definition explicitly states that reports to Congress or notifications are not participation, and merely making a report public after it is created does not involve the public in the *decision-making* process (i.e., consulting or coordinating with outsiders *before* a decision is made). The core actions here are internal agency directives and reporting.
